newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany mounts mass operation to hold back floods.
newsitem.headline: Germany mounts mass operation to hold back floods.

text.p: Thousands of troops worked round the clock in flood-hit east Germany on Thursday to shore up the banks of the River Oder in the German army's biggest ever peace-time operation since World War Two.

Officials warned 19,000 residents in the low-lying area of Oderbruch north of Frankfurt an der Oder to be ready for evacuation if more dikes reinforcing the banks burst, threatening to unleash the area's worst flooding in 50 years.

Defence Minister Volker Ruehe and Interior Minister Manfred Kanther, visiting the area bordering Poland, said the operation was a "challenge for all Germans" and a token of solidarity between the impoverished east and the more affluent west.

But officials said that despite the efforts of 8,300 soldiers and 600 border guards, water levels were rising steadily and could spark further floods that have already devastated parts of Poland and the Czech Republic.
"We must not be complacent," said Alwin Ziel, interior minister of Brandenburg, in a radio interview.
Ziel warned residents to brace for more floods, and a ministry spokesman said the dikes could collapse at any time.

Germany so far has escaped the worst of the flooding -- the most serious in centuries -- which claimed more than 100 lives and inundated thousands of homes earlier this month in the Czech Republic and Poland.

But German towns have been hit by power cuts and overflowing sewers, about 500 people have been ordered to leave from parts of the danger zone and farmers have started moving thousands of head of livestock.
Ziel praised the border guards and troops, saying that much of Germany's Oder region would already be under water without their efforts. "The German army is our mainstay in this crisis," Ziel said.
Officials said the situation remained critical, although new high water levels did not hit the region overnight as feared.
A spokesman for Ziel's ministry said water levels were rising slightly and experts expected a new high point to be reached around midnight.
The first dike on the Oder river burst on Wednesday south of Frankfurt. The interior ministry spokesman said water was pouring through a 300-metre (yard) wide hole in the dike.
But workers had been able to shore up another dike near the town of Eisenhuettenstadt, officials said, and no further evacuations were planned for the moment.
Kanther said officials would also be looking to see if lessons could be learned from the preparations for the arrival of the floods.
"We'll document very carefully what could be done better in the future," he told reporters during his visit.
Bonn has pledged to help the stricken area in every way possible and has earmarked a 200 million mark ($110 million) reconstruction fund for the area once the catastrophe was over.
